description:
We are Nexora, a team of curious and motivated students from Cochabamba, Bolivia, participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026!

We are passionate about technology, science, and solving real-world problems. We enjoy learning new things, sharing ideas, and turning challenges into practical solutions. Our work is built mainly with Python, which we use for data analysis, visualization, and building web applications.
summary:
Tunari Blindspot is a web application that harmonizes NASA FIRMS hot spot detections from MODIS and VIIRS over Tunari National Park, the mountain that surrounds Cochabamba, Bolivia.
The two sensors have different resolutions, formats and overpass times, so fire records are fragmented and often duplicated. Our tool merges both datasets into a single table, removes duplicate detections, and flags whether each hot spot was seen by both satellites or by only one.
Beyond harmonization, we measure how well each area is observed throughout the day, because a quiet spot on a map may simply mean that no satellite was watching. By combining historical fire recurrence with this observation coverage, the app highlights the sectors that deserve closer monitoring on the ground.
details:
What it does and how it works?
Tunari Blindspot harmonizes hot spot detections from two NASA satellite instruments, MODIS and VIIRS, over Tunari National Park in Cochabamba, Bolivia. The data comes from NASA FIRMS.
Benefits and intended impact:
A map without detections is often read as a safe area, but it may simply be an area that no satellite was watching. By showing these observation gaps, our tool helps park authorities, firefighters and land managers decide where to focus ground patrols and prevention efforts. It gives them one consistent picture instead of two fragmented records. The result is a monitoring priority map.
Tools and technologies:
Python, pandas, GeoPandas and PyArrow for data processing; Streamlit for the web application; Folium and Plotly for interactive maps and charts; Git and GitHub for teamwork. We used open NASA FIRMS data and standard laptops, with no special hardware.
How it is creative?
Most approaches stop at merging the data. We also measure what the satellites cannot see, turning the observation gaps themselves into useful information for decision making.
Factors our team considered
Data quality: MODIS reports confidence as a percentage and VIIRS as categories, so we standardized them.

  • Time: satellite data is recorded in UTC, so we display local Bolivian time.
  • Honesty: we present priority as a guide for monitoring, not as a prediction.
  • Accessibility: a colorblind-friendly palette, text descriptions for charts and a responsive layout.
  • Teamwork: four defined roles, separate Git branches and shared data files with agreed columns. - Scalability: the app reads standard files, so real data can be swapped in easily.
